_comment: How each place of the catalogue's words-12.jsonl was settled before it went in config/figures-seen/: two readers read every place against its BSB verse, one asking whether the figure is plainly there and one whether the marked words, form and tags are right; a place both passed is kept as handed over, and any place either questioned was read a third time and kept, changed or dropped. A new form stands only where a reader proposed it. Places not read are held, not listed. Stray punctuation before marked words is trimmed, and Strong's tags that light the article (G3588) or the object marker (H0853), or number eight, the search's limit, are taken off as a stretch of words.

Then kept figures of speech were read again by two readers, a third settling any difference ("words re-read" counts them: those a sample showed at risk, such as wide spans, or those found only in the Hebrew or Greek that carry no tags): each kept as it was, cut to the words that carry the figure, or dropped ("words").

Last, a sample of 25 kept places was read by two more readers, a third settling any split; the file goes in only when 24 or more pass, and any place that fails is dropped. "samples" lists each sample and its result.
A place whose verse already has the same form from an earlier file is left out here, since the earlier file's place stands ("same form already on this verse").

places.why: Jacob, afraid, cries "How awesome is this place!", a plain exclamation. The stray opening quotation mark is removed from the span.
Leah's "How fortunate!" is a plain cry of feeling. The stray opening quotation mark is removed.
Leah's "How happy I am!" is a plain cry of joy. The stray opening quotation mark is removed.

"I await Your salvation, O LORD." is a quiet statement ending in a period, with no cry or interjection in the BSB. Only Clarke calls it an ejaculation. A prayer to God present is not plainly apostrophe either, so it does not go live.
"Ah" (Hebrew 'oy, tagged H0188, the right word) is the cry. "who" begins the question that follows and is not part of the exclamation, so only "Ah" is marked.

"O foolish and senseless people" is an ordinary address inside the question "Is this how you repay the LORD...?", punctuated as a question, not a cry, and the span "O foolish" cuts the phrase in half. The rhetorical question is a different place at different words, not this one.
Michal's scornful "How the king of Israel has distinguished himself today!" is a plain exclamation. The stray opening quotation mark is removed.
David "cried out, 'O my son Absalom!'", a plain cry of grief. The span "O my son" split the cry from the name, so it now marks the whole first cry "O my son Absalom!".
The king "cried out at the top of his voice, 'O my son Absalom!'", a plain exclamation. The span now covers the whole cry, not just "O my son".

Elisha "cried out, 'My father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel!'", a plain cry. It has no interjection, so the exclamation is the whole cry. "My father, my father" alone is the span for doubling.
Jehoash wept over Elisha, "saying, 'My father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel!'", a plain cry of grief. As at 2 Kings 2:12, the exclamation is the whole cry.

The BSB sets "(though You, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserve...)" as a calm aside in brackets, with no cry or exclamation mark. Only Keil reads it as an exclamation, and the span stops mid-clause at "less".
Job's mocking "How you have helped the powerless and saved the arm that is feeble!" is a plain exclamation across both poetry lines. The stray opening quotation mark is removed.
same form already on this verse (job-34-7-question-seen)
"How awesome are Your deeds!" is a plain cry of praise. The marked words opened with a stray quotation mark, so they are given without it.

The verse goes on from 89:50's "Remember, O Lord, the reproach of Your servants...", and its lower-case "how" renders the Hebrew asher ("which"), a relative word. The line says what the reproach was, the thing the Lord is asked to remember. It is not plainly a separate cry.

"Oh, how I love Your law!" is a plain cry. The Hebrew carries it in mah ("how!"), which the BSB gives as "how", not in the added "Oh" alone. Mark the whole cry, as the other exclamation places in this file are marked.
"How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof!" is a plain cry of regret. The marked words opened with a stray quotation mark, so they are given without it.

"O my son" is an ordinary form of address inside the question "What shall I say, O my son?". It is not a cry of feeling. Whatever figure the verse has rests on the threefold "What", not on these words.

The tag H0337 rightly sits on ve'ilo ("and woe to him"), and the BSB gives it as a cry ending in "!": "but pity the one who falls...!". But "but" is only the joining word and does not carry the cry, so the marked word is "pity".

Line 3, "O wretched Anathoth!", has no verb. It is a cry of pity for the town, Hebrew 'aniyah, "O afflicted one". But marking only "O wretched" cuts the cry off from the town it mourns, so the span is the whole line without the closing mark.
"Woe to you, O Ariel" is a plain cry, and the tag H1945 is on hoy. The cry itself is "Woe". "to you" only names who it is aimed at, so the span is "Woe", as in the other woe places.
"Woe to the rebellious children" is a plain cry, and H1945 is on hoy. The marked "Woe to" ends on a dangling preposition, so the span is "Woe".

"How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news" is a plain exclamation of the "How...!" kind. Line 1 alone leaves out what is beautiful, so the span runs through "good news".

Hoy here is a summons, "Ho, all who thirst". It is not an outburst of feeling, and the BSB words for it are "Come", which a reader takes only as an invitation. "Come" also stands capitalized twice in the verse. The figure is not plain.

"Like ravenous dogs, they are never satisfied. They are shepherds with no discernment..." is plain statement with no cry in it. The place rests only on a commentator's note, and the span is the whole verse.

"How I long to make you My sons... of all the nations!" is a plain cry of longing; the Hebrew 'eikh ("how!") shows it too. The marked words began with a stray opening quote mark, so the span starts at "How".

"Woe is me, for my soul faints before the murderers!" is a plain cry, and H0188 is on 'oy. The marked pieces "Woe", "me" and "for my" were broken up, and "for my" belongs to the reason clause. The span is "Woe is me".

The BSB gives a plain statement of grief, "My sorrow is beyond healing; my heart is faint within me." It has no cry word and no exclamation mark. Only a commentator's reading of the Hebrew makes it an exclamation, so the figure is not plain in the verse.
The quoted wail "How devastated we are! How great is our shame!" is plainly a cry of feeling. The marked words began with a stray opening quotation mark, which is dropped here.

"Listen!" calls the hearer to an alarm. It is not plainly a cry of feeling, and only a commentator's note calls it an exclamation. The marked words are also the whole verse, most of it plain prediction ("The cities of Judah will be made a desolation"). When in doubt, it does not go live.
build would refuse: "you" starts or ends inside a word
build would refuse: "his" starts or ends inside a word
"Oh, Lord GOD!" is a plain outcry, and H0162 is tagged on 'ahah, the cry word. The second mark, "Lord", belongs to the address and carries no cry, so only "Oh" is kept.
The mourners' lament "Alas, O master!" is plainly a cry, and H1945 is tagged on hoy. The second mark, "O", is a piece of the address cut off from "master" and carries nothing, so only "Alas" is kept.

"Woe is me because the LORD has added sorrow to my pain!" is a plain cry of lament, and H0188 is tagged on 'oy. The mark "Woe is" stops halfway through the phrase, so the cry word "Woe" is marked on its own, as at the other Woe places.
"How shattered it is! How they wail! How Moab has turned his back in shame!" is plainly a run of cries. The marked words began with a stray opening quotation mark, which is dropped here.

The line "See, O LORD, how distressed I am!" is a plea asking God to see, and "how distressed I am" is what He is asked to see. It is not plainly an exclamation figure. The marked words also cut off "See,", which changes the sentence. When in doubt, it does not go live.

"How weak-willed is your heart" is a plain exclamation of reproach. The marked words ran on through the formula "declares the Lord GOD" and the clause after it, so they are cut back to the cry itself.
"You adulterous wife!" is a plain outburst of reproach. The marked words "You adulterous" stopped before "wife", the word the cry is about, so the whole cry is marked.

The BSB has no outcry here ("Yes, it is ready to flash like lightning"). The cry the search found is only in the Hebrew 'ach, which no Strong's tag marks, and the marked words are the whole verse. The figure cannot be seen in the words shown.

"Because you exclaimed, 'Aha!'" plainly quotes the Ammonites' gloating cry, and H1889 is tagged on he'ach. The second mark, "when", is no part of the cry and occurs three times in the verse, so only "Aha" is kept.

"Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves!" is a plain outcry, and H1945 is tagged on hoy. The second mark, "to", is a stray single word, so only the cry word "Woe" is kept, as at the other Woe places.
"Yes, woe be to them when I turn away from them!" is a plain cry of woe, and H0188 sits on 'oy "woe!". "be" is a supplied linking word, so the mark should be "woe" alone.
Ephraim's boast "How rich I have become!" is a plain exclamation. The marked words began with a stray opening quotation mark, so they are given without it.
"Woe is me!" is a plain cry and is its own poetry line. H0480 sits on 'allelay "woe!". "Woe is" cut the cry in half, so the mark becomes the whole cry, "Woe is me!".
found only in the Hebrew or Greek, and its tags are a stretch of words

"You brood of vipers, who warned you...?" is a form of address that leads straight into a question. The BSB does not set it apart as an outcry, so it is not plainly an exclamation. The figure in these words is the picture of vipers, and this file already has a place for that on the same words (matthew-3-7-hypocatastasis-seen, "brood of vipers"). Moving this place to metaphor would mark the same words twice.

"You brood of vipers, how can you who are evil say anything good?" is an address that opens a question, not an outcry set apart, so it is not plainly an exclamation. The vipers figure already has its own place in this file (matthew-12-34-hypocatastasis-seen, "brood of vipers"), so moving this one to metaphor would mark the same words twice.

In "You hypocrites, why are you testing Me?", "You hypocrites" is a word of address that runs into a question, not an outcry set apart. "hypocrites" has its ordinary meaning, so no figure is plain at these words.

The master's "Well done, good and faithful servant!" is a plain cry of approval. The marked words were the whole verse, with the narration and the plain statements after it. I narrowed them to the cry, the same span as 25:23.
build would refuse: tag G1436 is not the root of a word in the verse
"Isaiah prophesied correctly about you hypocrites" is a plain statement. "you hypocrites" is the object of "about", not a cry, so the marked words show no exclamation.
"O unbelieving generation!", followed by "How long must I remain with you?", is a plain outburst of grief. The marked "O unbelieving" stopped before the noun, so the span is now the whole cry.

"How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God!", said as the rich man goes away in sorrow, is a plain exclamation. The marked words began with a stray opening quotation mark, which is now dropped.
same form already on this verse (mark-15-34-doubling-seen)

"You brood of vipers, who warned you...?" is an address that opens a question. The BSB does not set it as a cry. What the words plainly carry is a metaphor: the crowds ("You") are called a brood of vipers. I marked the words used for something else. Note: place 324 (luke-3-7-hypocatastasis-seen) marks the same "brood of vipers". Because "You" names the people, metaphor is the better form, and the two should not both go live.

The demon's "Ha!" (Greek ea, tagged G1436) is a plain interjection, and the tag points at that very word. The marked words were the whole verse with its opening quotation mark. I narrowed them to "Ha!", with its mark, because a bare "Ha" would also match inside "Have".
"O unbelieving and perverse generation!" is a plain outburst before "How long must I remain with you". The marked "O unbelieving" cut the phrase off, so the span is now the whole cry.

"O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, ... but you were unwilling!" is a plain cry of lament. The marked words left out the "O" that makes it a cry, and without it they are only the doubled name. The span is now "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem".
"How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God!", said on seeing the man's sadness, is a plain exclamation. The marked words began with a stray opening quotation mark, which is now dropped.
"O foolish ones, how slow are your hearts to believe...!" is a plain outburst. The marked "O foolish" dropped the noun the cry belongs to, so the span is now "O foolish ones".
In the BSB, "How dare you insult the high priest of God!" is plainly a cry of indignation at Paul's words. The marked words began with a stray opening quotation mark, which is now dropped.

"But thanks be to God that, though you once were slaves to sin, you wholeheartedly obeyed..." is a thanksgiving built into an ordinary sentence with a "that" clause and a full stop. It carries the argument on and is not set off as a cry. With no source behind it, this is too doubtful to go live.
"How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!" is plainly a cry of feeling. The marked words began with a stray opening quotation mark, so I removed it.
"But thanks be to God, who always leads us..." is set as a statement that opens a long sentence of teaching. It is a thanksgiving, not plainly a cry of feeling.
"But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus..." is a calm statement of thanks about Titus, ending in a period. It is not plainly an outburst.
"O foolish Galatians!" is plainly a cry of feeling. The marked "O foolish" stopped before the word the cry is made to, so the cry is now marked whole.
"O foolish man, do you want evidence..." addresses the man before a question, with a comma. The BSB does not set it as a cry, and the marked "O foolish" cuts off "man".

The riddle is Samson's (14:14). "What is sweeter than honey? And what is stronger than a lion?" is the men's answer to it, as Samson's "you would not have solved my riddle" shows. These questions give the answer (honey, a lion) and ask nothing, so the figure is a question that is not asking, carried by both questions.

"The leech has two daughters: Give and Give" is a picture of greed that never has enough, and the next line ("three things that are never satisfied") opens it at once. Nothing in the verse sets it as a puzzle to be worked out. Calling it a riddle comes from the search's commentary.

"Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees" is a warning, not a riddle posed to be solved. The leaven stands for something left unnamed here, and 16:12 says it was "the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees". That is a likeness implied, carried by these words.

In "Destroy this temple", "this temple" stands for His body, which is not named here. 2:21 says so: "He was speaking about the temple of His body". That is a likeness implied on "this temple", not a riddle.

In "I have food to eat that you know nothing about", "food" stands for something left unnamed. 4:34 names it: "My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me". That is a likeness implied on "food", not a riddle.
"You will look for Me, but you will not find Me" follows the plain words of 7:33 ("I am going to the One who sent Me"). The hearers misread a plain saying. No puzzle is set to be worked out.
"Where I am going, you cannot come" is a plain statement that the hearers misread ("Will He kill Himself?", 8:22). The text does not set it as a riddle.
"In a little while you will see Me no more..." is a prediction in plain words that puzzles the disciples (16:17-18). That does not plainly make it a riddle posed to be solved. In doubt, it stays out.

In "Many bulls surround me; strong bulls of Bashan encircle me", the enemies are given only as bulls and are not named. The figure is carried by the bulls. "surround me" and "encircle me" are what the enemies do, so they are left out.

places.words_why: In "my precious life from the power of wild dogs" the picture is the "wild dogs", put for his enemies without naming them, as 22:16 sets "dogs surround me" beside "a band of evil men". "power" is not part of that picture.

places.why: In "Save me from the mouth of the lion; at the horns of the wild oxen", the enemies are given only as a lion and wild oxen. "Save me from" is the prayer, not the picture. The picture is the lion and the oxen.
The enemies who "gnashed their teeth at me" (35:16) are given only as "these lions". The leading preposition "from" is not part of the figure.

"My soul is among the lions" gives only the picture of fierce foes. The line itself never says they are lions, and they are named only later in the verse. The figure is carried by "the lions", not by "My soul is among".

In "the herd of bulls among the calves of the nations", the thing meant is partly named ("of the nations"), so the likeness is not left wholly implied. The marked span cuts the phrase before "of the nations". Who the "bulls" are cannot be seen from the verse without a commentary. In doubt, so it fails.

"The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone" gives only the picture. Who the stone and the builders stand for is left implied. The picture runs through both lines, so the cornerstone is now marked too.

places.words_why: "a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse" pictures a coming son of Jesse's line, whom 11:2 calls "Him". The figure is in the plant words "a shoot" and "the stump of Jesse", not the verb; the marking is kept to line 1 as before.
Against "Me, the fountain of living water", "they have dug their own cisterns" pictures what they turned to without naming it. The figure is in "their own cisterns", not the verb "dug".

places.why: In "Many shepherds have destroyed My vineyard", the rulers and the LORD's land are given only as shepherds and a vineyard. The marked words stopped before "My vineyard", which is half the picture. "have destroyed" is the act, not the figure.
The men who will seize the people are given only as fishermen who "catch them" and hunters who "hunt them down". They are not named. "send for" is the LORD's own act, not the figure.

The BSB names who is meant right beside the picture: "you cows of Bashan on Mount Samaria, you women who oppress the poor". So the likeness is not left implied. The women are called cows of Bashan, which is a metaphor.

"Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered" pictures the leader struck and his people scattered. The people are left unnamed as "the sheep". The marked "Strike the Shepherd" dropped the sheep half of the picture, and "Strike" is the sword's act.
In "You brood of vipers", John speaks "to them" and names them "You". The people are named and called vipers, so this is a stated metaphor, not a likeness left implied.

places.words_why: "His winnowing fork is in His hand to clear His threshing floor... gather His wheat... burn up the chaff" plainly pictures the Coming One's judgment. The figure is in the picture's nouns, not in "is in His hand".

places.why: "I will make you fishers of men" names both the men ("you") and what they will be. Said to fishermen casting a net, it is plainly a metaphor, not an implied likeness.

The verse names the thing first ("You are the salt of the earth"), so the salt that follows carries on a stated metaphor, not an implied one. A cited metaphor place already marks "You are the salt of the earth". The span "salt loses its" also breaks off before "savor".
The dead cannot bury anyone, so the first "the dead" plainly pictures living people, and what it means is left unnamed. "bury their own dead" is literal, so only "the dead" carries the figure.

Asked why He eats with sinners, Jesus answers only with a picture of a doctor and the sick. 9:13 makes plain that He is the doctor and the sinners are the sick. The span should be the whole saying, not a fragment that starts at "not".
places.words_why: Asked why He eats with sinners, Jesus answers "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick", plainly picturing Himself as the doctor and sinners as the sick. The figure is in the three nouns, not the whole clause.

Right after the crowds are seen "like sheep without a shepherd" (v36), "The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few" plainly pictures the people as a harvest and those sent as workers, as v38 confirms ("send out workers into His harvest"). The picture is carried by "The harvest" and "the workers", not by "is plentiful".

places.why: same form already on this verse (matthew-12-20-hypocatastasis-seen)

places.words_why: "Make a tree good and its fruit will be good ... for a tree is known by its fruit" comes in a rebuke of the Pharisees and leads into "out of the overflow of the heart, the mouth speaks" (v34), so the tree and its fruit plainly picture a man and what comes from him. The picture is carried by "a tree" and "its fruit", not by the verb "Make" or "good".

places.why: "You brood of vipers, how can you who are evil" names the hearers ("You") and calls them vipers. Both are given, so it is a stated metaphor.

She takes up Jesus' picture from 15:26 ("toss it to the dogs"). She is one of the dogs and asks for a crumb, and none of this is said outright. The whole clause is the picture; "even the dogs eat" stops before the crumbs.
places.words_why: The woman takes up Jesus' picture: "even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their master's table". She and her need are plainly pictured. The figure is in the nouns, not the whole clause.

places.why: "I was not telling you about bread" shows the leaven is a picture, and 16:12 names its meaning. "beware of" is the literal warning, so only "the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees" carries the figure.
"If your hand or your foot causes you to sin" speaks of the body's own members. Nothing plainly makes them a picture of something left unnamed, so there is no implied likeness at these words.
"if your eye causes you to sin" names the eye itself. The verse does not plainly make it a picture of something else.

places.words_why: "You strain out a gnat but swallow a camel" is plainly a picture of 23:23: they tithe mint but neglect justice. The figure is both halves, so the camel has to be marked as well as the gnat.

places.why: "You snakes! You brood of vipers!" calls the scribes and Pharisees, named as "You", vipers. Both are named, so it is a stated metaphor.

"Wherever there is a carcass, there the vultures will gather" is a saying, and a cited proverb place already marks it. The verse does not make plain what the carcass and vultures stand for, so an implied likeness is not plain. The span also leaves out the saying's first half.

places.words_why: "You will all fall away on account of Me. For it is written: 'I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered'" plainly makes the Shepherd Jesus and the sheep the disciples. The figure is in the Shepherd and the sheep, not in the verb "strike".

places.why: Asked why He eats with sinners, Jesus answers with a picture of a doctor and the sick. "I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners" shows what it means. The span should be the whole saying, not a fragment that leaves out "but the sick".

places.words_why: In "the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast", the bridegroom is plainly Jesus, as in 2:19. The figure is "the bridegroom", not the verb "will be taken" beside it.

Jesus gives "No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment" as part of His answer about fasting, between the bridegroom and the wineskins, so it is plainly a picture and not advice about mending. The picture is new cloth set against an old garment, so the marked words need the garment too. I left out the "a" to keep the marked words short.

Spoken to "a Greek woman" (7:26), "it is not right to take the children's bread and toss it to the dogs" is plainly a picture of Israel and the Gentiles. The figure is in "the children's bread" and "the dogs", not in the verb "toss it".

places.why: She takes up the picture from 7:27 ("toss it to the dogs") and leaves its meaning unnamed. The whole clause is the picture; "even the dogs under" breaks off on a preposition.
places.words_why: She answers inside Jesus' picture: "even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs". The figure is carried by the dogs and the children's crumbs, not by the verb "eat".

places.why: 8:16-21 show the leaven is not bread ("Do you not yet understand?"), and its meaning is left unnamed. "Beware of" is the literal warning, so only "the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod" carries the figure.
"If your hand causes you to sin" names the hand itself. Nothing plainly makes it a picture of something left unnamed.
"If your foot causes you to sin" names the foot itself. Nothing plainly makes it a picture of something else.
"if your eye causes you to sin" names the eye itself. The verse does not plainly make it a picture of something left unnamed.

"Have salt among yourselves, and be at peace with one another" plainly makes salt a picture of something in the disciples that is never named. A separate proverb place already marks "if the salt loses its saltiness", and "salt loses its" breaks off before "saltiness".
places.words_why: "Have salt among yourselves, and be at peace with one another" plainly does not mean literal salt. The figure is the salt the disciples are to have, not the verb "Have".

"You will all fall away, for it is written: 'I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered'" plainly makes Jesus the Shepherd and the disciples the sheep. The figure is in those two words, not in the verb "strike".

places.why: Coming after "Produce fruit... in keeping with repentance" (3:8), the axe at the root of the trees plainly pictures judgment on the people, who are not named. The span should take in "of the trees".

places.words_why: John is speaking of the One who "will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire", and "His winnowing fork is in His hand ... He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire" is plainly a picture of judgment. The current marked words take in the verb "is in His hand", so they are cut to the picture word alone, keeping the fewest words that still show the figure.

places.why: The verse itself names it: "you will quote this proverb to Me: 'Physician, heal yourself!'" The form is proverb, and the marked words are exactly the proverb.
Asked why He eats with sinners (5:30), Jesus answers only with a picture of doctor and sick, and 5:32 makes the meaning plain. The span must be the whole saying, including "but the sick".
places.words_why: In reply to "Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?", Jesus gives only the picture, "the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick", and 5:32 ("I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners") shows what it means. "It is not" is just the sentence frame, so it is cut.
"the bridegroom will be taken from them" plainly points to Jesus, following on from 5:34. The figure is carried by "the bridegroom", not by the verb.

places.why: The wineskins saying continues what 5:36 introduces in so many words: "He also told them a parable". The text names the form, so it is parable. The marked words are the picture.
The verse says "Jesus also told them a parable", so the form is parable. The parable is the whole two-question picture, not a fragment of the first question.
The speck and the beam picture faults that are never named. The marked words cut "brother's" in the middle and drop "eye", so the span should be the two pictured parts.

places.words_why: In "Let the dead bury their own dead" the first "the dead" must mean living people who are dead in another sense, since the dead cannot bury anyone. Those are the words that carry the figure.

places.why: This answers the man who wants to say farewell first (9:61). Plowing and looking back picture starting to follow and then turning back, and that meaning is left implied. The looking back is the point, so it belongs in the span.

places.words_why: As He sends the seventy-two "to every town and place", "The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few" plainly pictures the people to be reached and those sent to them ("send out workers into His harvest"). The figure is in "The harvest" and "the workers". "is plentiful" is only what is said about them.

places.why: The disciples are addressed only by the picture "little flock". "Do not be afraid" does not carry the figure.
"that fox" is Herod (named in 13:31), called only by the picture word. "tell" is not part of the figure.

The saying comes right after the cost of being "My disciple" (14:33) and closes with "He who has ears to hear" (14:35), so salt plainly pictures the disciple, who is not named. The marked words stop before "savor".
places.words_why: Coming among the sayings on discipleship and followed by "He who has ears to hear, let him hear", "the salt loses its savor" is plainly a picture, not a kitchen fact. The "if" beside it is dropped.

places.why: "Where, Lord?" is answered only with a picture whose meaning is left implied. Without the carcass half, "there" points at nothing, so the span should be the whole saying.
The green tree and the dry one are a picture whose meaning is left implied. The figure lies in setting green against dry, and "tree is green" alone reads as literal.
places.words_why: No tree is in view in "if men do these things while the tree is green, what will happen when it is dry?", so the green tree and the dry tree are plainly a picture whose meaning is left unsaid. The two phrases carry the figure, so "while" and "what will happen when" are cut.

places.why: "food" stands for doing the Father's will, which is not named here. The disciples take it literally (4:33), and 4:34 explains it. "that you know nothing about" does not carry the figure.

Right after "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified" (12:23), the kernel that dies and bears fruit plainly pictures His death without naming it. The span stopped at "falls" and dropped the dying and the fruit, which are the point.
places.words_why: Coming right after "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified" and before "Whoever loves his life will lose it", "a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies ... it bears much fruit" plainly pictures His death without naming it. Since fewer marked words is the safer choice, the marking is cut to the picture's two halves, leaving out "unless" and "if it dies".

places.why: Leaven pictures the sin being tolerated, which goes unnamed here, and 5:7 makes it plain ("Get rid of the old leaven"). The span stopped in mid-clause.
Placed between "Such persuasion" (5:8) and "The one who is troubling you" (5:10), the leaven plainly pictures the false teaching, which is never named. The span stopped in mid-clause.
"those dogs" is a picture for the evil workers, who are not named by it, and the parallel "those workers of evil" shows that people are meant. "Watch out for" is not part of the figure.
Speaking of his first defense (4:16), Paul pictures the deadly danger as the lion's mouth and leaves the danger unnamed. "delivered from" is the literal act, not the figure.
Listed with sorcerers, murderers and idolaters, "the dogs" plainly means a kind of person who is never named. "outside are" does not carry the figure.
